title: Winston Churchill and Clement Attlee: Fierce Rivals in Commons, Staunch Partners in Nationhood
summary: Though ideological adversaries who fought bitter postwar elections, conservative Winston Churchill and socialist Clement Attlee exemplified the finest traditions of democratic civility and mutual respect.
keywords: Winston Churchill and Lady Astor: Poison in the Coffee
full_text:
In the summer of 1945, having steered Great Britain through the darkest days of World War II in a national coalition government, Conservative Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Labour Deputy Prime Minister Clement Attlee faced each other as bitter opponents in the general election.

They presented an astonishing contrast in personal style: Churchill was a flamboyant, cigar-chomping aristocrat and oratorical volcano; Attlee was an understated, pipe-smoking social reformer whose quiet reserve was famously lampooned by Churchill: "He is a modest man, who has much to be modest about!"

To the shock of the world, British voters swept Labour into a landslide victory, making Attlee Prime Minister. It was Attlee's administration that subsequently enacted the National Health Service and legislated Indian independence in 1947.

Shortly after the transfer of power, the two political rivals bumped into each other inside the parliamentary washroom at Westminster. Churchill conspicuously took a sink several basins away.

Attlee looked over with an amused grin and asked:
"Winston, why are you keeping such a careful distance from me? Are we not still colleagues in this House?"

Churchill peered over his spectacles with twinkling mischief:
"Clement, whenever you see anything that is large, well-managed, and privately owned, you socialists insist upon nationalizing it and carving it up for the public! I am merely protecting my private enterprise!"

Attlee burst into chuckles, puffing contentedly on his briar pipe. Though they clashed fiercely on economic ideology, Churchill and Attlee shared deep mutual respect, proving that passionate political opposition need never destroy civil affection and democratic sportsmanship.

moral: Vigorous democratic contest must coexist with profound mutual respect; civility is the crowning virtue of public life.
moral_reflection: Sharp repartee turns hostility back upon the attacker.
